threads.topic: Short-term borrowing funding the schools deficit

entries.q: The treasury monitoring report says short-term debt has 'increased significantly to satisfy the cash demand of' the accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant deficit. How much of current short-term borrowing is attributable to the DSG deficit, what does it cost each year, and what is assumed to happen when the statutory override ends?
entries.why: Borrowing to cover a revenue deficit is not borrowing for capital: there is no asset and no MRP profile behind it, only a rolling refinancing at whatever short rates are on the day. The council's own chart puts the two lines side by side.

threads.topic: Five years and a fifth of the book to one council

entries.q: The strategy allows up to 20% of the portfolio with a single local authority for up to five years, against a two-year limit for AA- rated banks. What is the evidence base for treating an unrated council as a longer-dated risk than a rated bank?
entries.why: The council is simultaneously borrowing from the inter-authority market because it is cheap and lending into it because it pays well. Both sides of that trade rest on the same assumption about council credit.

threads.topic: The numbers are published as pictures

entries.q: Every numerical table in the treasury strategy and the monitoring report is published as an image rather than as text. Could future reports publish the tables as text or alongside a machine-readable version?
entries.why: A resident, a councillor using a screen reader, or anyone comparing BCP to its neighbours cannot select, search or copy a single figure from either paper. The reporting itself is thorough; only the format hides it.

summary.text:
Read, and largely unyielding — for a reason worth stating. We read two of BCP's treasury papers: the monitoring report to 31 December 2025 and the Treasury Management Strategy Statement for 2026/27. Both are the right papers. In both, every numerical table — the capital expenditure plans, the CFR projections, the authorised limit, the current portfolio, the borrowing and investment summaries — is published as an image rather than as text. The prose extracts; the figures do not. So this council's balance sheet is not recorded below, and that is a limitation of the published format, not a gap in the council's reporting.

What the prose does say is worth having. Treasury was forecasting a £1.1m underspend for 2025/26 — improved from £0.3m at Q2 — because the council has been borrowing from other local authorities at rates below short-term PWLB, saving around £0.6m in interest, and holding higher cash balances into April 2026 to lend back into the same market. Combined investments returned 4.16% against a 4.05% SONIA benchmark. The council maintains an under-borrowed position deliberately, on the expectation that longer-dated rates fall.

One line in the monitoring report deserves more attention than its placement suggests. A debt chart is included, at external audit's recommendation, overlaying borrowing since April 2022 with the accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant deficit over the same period — and the report states that short-term debt has 'increased significantly to satisfy the cash demand of the deficit'. That is short-term borrowing funding a revenue deficit, which is a different thing from borrowing for capital, and the statutory override that keeps DSG deficits off the General Fund does not run forever.

Two smaller things. Cumulative voluntary revenue provision overpayments between 1 April 2023 and 31 March 2025 were £12.8m — money charged above the statutory minimum, which the guidance allows to be reclaimed in later years and which therefore sits as a usable cushion. And the counterparty framework allows up to 20% with any one local authority for up to five years, which is generous next to the same council's two-year ceiling for AA- rated banks.
